recall_prompt: Say how you would resolve (x² − x + 1)/((x + 1)(x − 1)²) into partial fractions — name each move in order.
insider_note: The repeated factor needs both B/(x − 1) and C/(x − 1)² in the form; there is no third root, so B can only come from comparing the x² coefficients — no substitution will produce it.

steps.label: Set up the form
steps.margin_note: First mark. (x − 1)² is a REPEATED linear factor, so it needs two fractions: one over (x − 1) and one over (x − 1)². Three fractions in all.

recall.must_convey: That the repeated factor (x − 1)² gives two fractions, B/(x − 1) and C/(x − 1)², beside A/(x + 1).
accept: write A over x plus one plus B over x minus one plus C over x minus one squared because x minus one is repeated
the repeated factor needs both x minus one and x minus one squared in the denominators
three fractions A by x plus 1, B by x minus 1 and C by x minus 1 whole square
x minus one repeat avutundi kabatti B by x minus one plus C by x minus one square rasali, plus A by x plus one
one fraction for x plus one and two fractions for the repeated x minus one

steps.why: A repeated factor (x − 1)² contains two denominators, (x − 1) and (x − 1)². Writing only C/(x − 1)² leaves one fraction short and the identity cannot then be satisfied for every x.
common_mistakes: Writing only A/(x + 1) + C/(x − 1)² and missing the B/(x − 1) fraction.
Writing (Bx + C)/(x − 1)² instead of B/(x − 1) + C/(x − 1)²; both give the same result, but the split form is the one marked.
Expanding (x − 1)² to x² − 2x + 1 and treating it as an irreducible quadratic.

steps.label: Clear the denominators
steps.margin_note: Second mark. Multiply by (x + 1)(x − 1)². A keeps (x − 1)², B keeps (x + 1)(x − 1) because one (x − 1) cancels, and C keeps only (x + 1) because both cancel.

recall.must_convey: That multiplying through gives x² − x + 1 = A(x − 1)² + B(x + 1)(x − 1) + C(x + 1).
accept: multiply both sides by x plus one into x minus one squared to get x squared minus x plus one equals A into x minus one squared plus B into x plus one into x minus one plus C into x plus one
clear the denominators and the C term keeps only x plus one because both x minus one cancel
multiply through by the whole denominator to get an identity in x
denominator tho multiply cheste A into x minus one square plus B into x plus one x minus one plus C into x plus one vastundi
remove the fractions so each constant keeps what did not cancel
heard_as: A into x minus one squared

steps.why: The B fraction has one (x − 1) under it and the C fraction has two, so after multiplying by (x − 1)² the B term keeps one (x − 1) and the C term keeps none. Getting these leftover factors right is the whole of this step.
common_mistakes: Giving the C term (x + 1)(x − 1) instead of (x + 1).
Giving the B term (x − 1)² instead of (x + 1)(x − 1).
Dropping the left side x² − x + 1.

steps.label: Find the constants
steps.margin_note: Third mark. Only two roots, 1 and −1, but three constants. x = 1 gives C, x = −1 gives A, and B comes from comparing the x² coefficient on both sides.

recall.must_convey: That x = 1 gives C = 1/2, x = −1 gives A = 3/4, and comparing the x² coefficients gives A + B = 1, so B = 1/4.
accept: put x equals one to get C equals half, x equals minus one to get A equals three by four, then compare x squared to get A plus B equals one so B is one by four
two substitutions give C half and A three quarters and the x squared coefficient gives B one quarter
C is half A is three by four and B is one by four from the coefficient of x squared
x equals one pedithe C half, x equals minus one pedithe A three by four, x square coefficient compare cheste B one by four
the third constant comes from equating the x squared coefficients because there is no third root

steps.why: A repeated factor has only one root, so substitution gives fewer equations than there are constants. Equating the coefficient of x² on both sides is the extra equation; it works because an identity has equal coefficients term by term.
common_mistakes: Trying to find B by substitution; there is no third root, so no substitution isolates B.
Reading the x² coefficient on the right as A only and forgetting the B(x + 1)(x − 1) term also gives x².
Putting x = −1 and getting (−1)² − (−1) + 1 as 1 instead of 3.

steps.label: Write the result
steps.margin_note: Last mark. The three fractional constants go into the denominators: 3/(4(x + 1)), 1/(4(x − 1)), 1/(2(x − 1)²). Write the original fraction on the left.

accept: the answer is three over four x plus one plus one over four x minus one plus one over two x minus one squared
three by four into x plus one plus one by four into x minus one plus one by two into x minus one whole square
write three by four x plus 1 plus one by four x minus 1 plus one by two x minus 1 square as the answer
final answer three by four x plus one plus one by four x minus one plus one by two x minus one square ani rasali
put A B and C back into the three fractions and write the original fraction on the left

steps.why: The mark is for the resolved form with all three fractions, including the one over (x − 1)². A student who found the constants but wrote two fractions has not resolved the given fraction.
common_mistakes: Dropping the B/(x − 1) fraction in the final line after correctly finding B.
Writing 3/4 over (x + 1) as a stacked fraction instead of 3/(4(x + 1)).
Not checking: put x = 0 in the identity, 1 = 3/4 − 1/4 + 1/2. If the two sides differ, a constant is wrong.
